strengths: The proposed resource is potentially valuable in scale and scope: 2.7M clips (7,089 hours) with estimated camera poses, depth, dynamic masks, motion instructions, and structured semantic captions would substantially exceed most comparable spatial-video datasets.

The curation pipeline addresses several practical failure modes of web video through scene segmentation, aesthetic/luminance/OCR/motion filtering, pose-estimation checks, and construction of a more balanced HQ subset.

Combining geometric estimates with caption refinement is a sensible way to reduce directional camera-motion errors made by a vision-language model. The qualitative example demonstrates the intended benefit clearly.
The manuscript covers diverse real-world environments and reports useful corpus statistics, including motion, scene categories, caption lengths, and comparisons with Panda70M.
The overall pipeline and intended applications to reconstruction, controllable video generation, and embodied navigation are clearly motivated.
weaknesses: The central annotation-quality claim is not adequately validated. Camera poses, depth, masks, and captions are model-generated pseudo-labels, yet no quantitative evaluation against ground truth, calibrated human audit, uncertainty analysis, or error rate is reported. Figure 6 provides only selected trajectory visualizations without reference trajectories or numerical accuracy, so it cannot establish that MegaSaM is more accurate than the alternatives.

The paper presents no downstream experiment demonstrating that training with SpatialVID improves reconstruction, pose estimation, video generation, spatial reasoning, or generalization. Consequently, the abstract's claim that the dataset directly fosters improved model performance and generalization is unsupported by the reported evidence.

Several critical pipeline details are missing: pose/acceleration rejection formulas and thresholds, motion-instruction thresholds and smoothing, SAM2 prompting and temporal-consistency details, HQ sampling rules, category-balancing targets, and the precise modifications to MegaSaM and PySceneDetect. These omissions prevent reproduction and make it difficult to assess selection bias.

The dataset construction is heavily biased toward a small set of YouTube search concepts such as walking, house tours, driving, and drones. Moreover, videos dominated by moving foreground objects are explicitly removed. This weakens the repeated characterization of the corpus as broadly diverse dynamic scenes; much of the reported dynamism appears to be camera motion rather than complex scene dynamics.

The proposed trajectory statistics are underspecified and potentially unreliable. MoveDist is difficult to compare across monocular reconstructions without a clearly defined common metric scale; RotAngle does not specify a proper SO(3) computation; and counting local extrema relative to the start-end line can be unstable under noise or degenerate for loops. The acceleration-based plausibility test is also not formally described or empirically validated.

The comparison with Panda70M mainly shows distributions of metrics used to select SpatialVID-HQ, making the conclusion of superior quality partly circular. Caption-length increases and word clouds do not demonstrate caption correctness, spatial fidelity, or semantic diversity.

The manuscript does not clearly specify train/validation/test splits, source-level deduplication, leakage controls, annotation frame rate, or whether source videos and all annotations will actually be distributable. It also omits discussion of YouTube licensing, creator consent, privacy, and removal procedures, which are material concerns for a web-scale dataset.

Reported corpus counts are difficult to reconcile across the text and figures (for example, over 7M versus 6M preprocessed clips and approximately 3M versus 3.4M filtered clips). Numerous grammatical and typographic issues further reduce clarity, although these presentation problems are secondary to the validation and reproducibility gaps.

strengths: The proposed resource is potentially valuable in scale and scope: the manuscript reports 2.7M real-world clips totaling 7,089 hours, with camera poses, depth, dynamic masks, motion instructions, and structured captions, as well as a 1,146-hour balanced subset.
The curation pipeline combines several practically relevant quality controls, including aesthetics, luminance, OCR, motion, trajectory plausibility, and dynamic-region filtering.

The annotations are designed to support multiple computer-vision problems, including reconstruction, camera-controlled generation, and spatially grounded video understanding. The qualitative examples are visually clear, and comparison with existing datasets helps establish the intended niche.
The authors acknowledge several limitations of the MegaSaM-based reconstruction stage and attempt to improve its depth and dynamic-mask components using stronger pretrained models.
weaknesses: The paper provides no downstream experiment demonstrating that training with SpatialVID improves reconstruction, video generation, camera control, or spatial reasoning. Consequently, central claims that the dataset improves model generalization and performance are unsupported. This is a material validation gap for a dataset paper, not merely limited evaluation breadth.

Annotation accuracy is not quantitatively established. Figure 6 offers only trajectory visualizations without ground truth, error metrics, evaluation data, or runtime measurements, yet the text claims that MegaSaM is more accurate and achieves the best accuracy-speed balance. There is likewise no human or benchmark validation of depth, poses, dynamic masks, motion instructions, captions, or category tags.

The manuscript misleadingly refers to camera motion as “ground truth,” although poses and depth are outputs of pretrained monocular estimation systems. These pseudo-labels inherit model failures and monocular scale ambiguity. In particular, MoveDist comparisons are not meaningful unless trajectory scale is calibrated or normalized, which is not explained.

The Panda-70M comparison largely measures properties explicitly optimized by the authors’ collection and filtering criteria. The tested split size is not reported, more than 80% of Panda clips are classified as unreconstructable by the authors’ own estimator, and no uncertainty or significance analysis is given. Compact distributions of aesthetic, luminance, and motion scores do not by themselves establish superior annotation quality or downstream utility.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Important implementation details are missing, including acceleration rejection criteria, smoothing and motion-label thresholds, trajectory-scale handling, the exact motion-score computation, sampling quotas, prompts, decoding settings, caption-quality controls, and details of the claimed MegaSaM adjustments. Several counts are also difficult to reconcile, such as over seven million preprocessed clips versus six million in Figure 3 and approximately 3–3.4M clips after filtering.

The contribution is primarily large-scale engineering that composes existing estimators and language models with straightforward filters. That can still be worthwhile, but without accuracy validation or utility experiments, the manuscript does not show that its scale translates into a reliable scientific resource.

The paper does not provide a concrete release and access plan, standardized train/validation/test splits, or sufficient discussion of YouTube licensing, redistribution permissions, privacy, identifiable individuals, geographic bias, and the terms governing generated annotations. These omissions materially undermine usefulness and reproducibility at the claimed scale.

Presentation needs substantial editing: some claims exceed the evidence, terminology such as “dynamic” conflates scene dynamics with camera motion, and numerous grammatical errors and unexplained inconsistencies obscure the technical account. These issues are secondary to the missing validation but further reduce confidence in the work.

strengths: SpatialVID is potentially a valuable resource: it contains 2.7M clips (7,089 hours and 127.6M frames), substantially exceeding most spatially annotated video datasets listed in Table 1.

The dataset combines unusually broad supervision—camera poses, depth, dynamic masks, motion instructions, and structured semantic captions—within one coherent pipeline. This could support reconstruction, camera-controlled generation, and spatial video understanding.

The collection and filtering process is thoughtfully motivated. Motion-oriented source selection, scene segmentation, aesthetic/luminance/OCR/motion filtering, and the balanced 1,146-hour SpatialVID-HQ subset address practical deficiencies of generic web-video corpora.

Incorporating estimated camera trajectories into caption refinement is a sensible idea. The example in Figure 9 clearly illustrates how geometric information can correct a VLM's erroneous motion direction.

The manuscript is generally easy to follow and provides informative dataset statistics, qualitative examples, comparisons with existing datasets, and useful disclosure of the substantial computational cost of annotation.
weaknesses: The central weakness is insufficient validation of annotation correctness. Camera poses and depth are pseudo-labels produced by a modified MegaSaM pipeline, yet the abstract refers to ground-truth camera motion. Figure 6 provides only qualitative trajectory visualizations and no pose/depth errors, failure rates, uncertainty estimates, or evaluation against videos with known geometry. Consequently, the reliability of the dataset's most important annotations is not established.

No downstream experiment demonstrates that training with SpatialVID improves reconstruction, camera-motion estimation, video generation, or spatial reasoning. The comparison with Panda-70M measures distributions of filtering or trajectory statistics rather than task utility. Given the paper's claims that the data improve generalization and performance, this missing evidence is material rather than merely a request for broader evaluation.

Other generated annotations are also largely unvalidated. There is no human audit or benchmark for dynamic masks, motion instructions, captions, or semantic tags. The captioning evidence consists principally of one favorable example, while caption length and word-frequency plots do not measure accuracy. SAM2 refinement can improve mask boundaries but does not by itself verify that MegaSaM's motion cues identify the correct dynamic objects.

Important technical details needed for reproducibility are absent: the MegaSaM modifications, acceleration-based rejection rule, smoothing filters, pose-change thresholds, instruction serialization, prompts, sampling policy, and HQ thresholds are not specified precisely. The representation through which numerical poses are supplied to Qwen is also unclear.

Monocular scale handling is insufficiently explained. MoveDist and translation thresholds assume comparable trajectory scales, but monocular pose estimation is generally scale-ambiguous. Although metric-depth models are introduced, the manuscript does not establish how scale is recovered, calibrated, or made comparable across clips.

The collection is strongly biased toward motion-search terms and particular sources—walking, house tours, driving, and drones dominate—and videos with substantial foreground dynamics are manually excluded. This makes the repeated characterization as broadly dynamic potentially misleading: the corpus appears rich in camera motion but comparatively selective about independently moving objects.

Dataset accessibility and governance are unclear. The manuscript does not provide a release link, licensing terms, redistribution plan, train/validation/test splits, deduplication procedure, or privacy/copyright safeguards for the YouTube-derived content. There are also reporting inconsistencies, including more than seven million versus six million preprocessed clips and three million versus 3.4 million filtered clips.

Overall, the scale and annotation breadth make the work promising, but the lack of quantitative annotation validation and downstream evidence leaves the main scientific claims insufficiently supported. These concerns place the submission near the decision boundary rather than supporting a clear acceptance recommendation.
